children.title: INTRODUCTION TO TRANSFORMERS
children.summary: This page is the title slide for a presentation titled 'INTRODUCTION TO TRANSFORMERS' by Jesús Cerquides from IIIA-CSIC, dated 2/07/2024. It is part of the 'Escuela AI HUB de verano' (Summer School on AI and Education). The slide features logos of sponsoring organizations including CSIC, Fundación 'la Caixa', IFIC, and Universitat de València.

children.title: Interests
children.summary: The section titled 'Interests' lists the professional research interests of Jesus Cerquides. The key topics include AI for Participatory Sciences & Democracy, Probabilistic Graphical Models, Causal Inference, Machine Learning in Health, and Quantum Machine Learning.

children.title: Academia
children.summary: The 'Academia' section lists the educational background of Jesus Cerquides, detailing his degrees in Computer Science (M.Sc.), Mathematics (Degree), and Artificial Intelligence (Ph.D.) from BarcelonaTech and UAB, along with associated prizes and years.

children.title: News
children.summary: The 'News' section is titled and contains the subtitle 'Latest things I have been doing', but no specific news items or content are visible in the provided image.

children.title: What I hope you will learn
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/What I hope you will learn
children.summary: This page is a presentation slide titled 'What I hope you will learn', outlining the learning objectives for a session on Transformers. The content lists four key topics: an introduction to transformers and composites, the main tasks solvable with transformers, how these tasks are solved using transformer constructs and layers, and an internal look at how transformer layers function.

children.title: Prehistoric Era
children.summary: The 'Prehistoric Era' section covers the period from the 1990s, characterized by rule-based methods, parsing, RNNs, and LSTMs.

children.title: Simple attention mechanisms
children.summary: The section titled 'Simple attention mechanisms' is a timeline entry for the year 2014, marking the emergence of simple attention mechanisms in the history of AI.

children.title: Beginning of transformers
children.summary: The section titled "Beginning of transformers" marks the year 2017 on the timeline and highlights the publication of the paper "Attention is all you need" as the starting point for transformer models.

children.title: Explosion of transformers in NLP
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Attention Timeline/Explosion of transformers in NLP
children.summary: The section titled 'Explosion of transformers in NLP' marks the year 2018 on the timeline. It highlights this period as a significant expansion of transformer models within Natural Language Processing, specifically citing BERT and GPT-3 as key examples.

children.title: Explosion into other fields
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Attention Timeline/Explosion into other fields
children.summary: This section covers the period from 2018 to 2020, marking the expansion of transformer models beyond Natural Language Processing (NLP) into other domains. It specifically highlights the emergence of Vision Transformers (ViTs) and AlphaFold-2 as key developments during this time.

children.title: Start of Generative Era
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Attention Timeline/Start of Generative Era
children.summary: The section titled 'Start of Generative Era' covers the period from 2021 to 2022. It highlights key developments and models that emerged during this time, including Codex, Decision Transformers, GPT-X, and DALL-E.

children.title: Present Day
children.summary: The 'Present Day' section, corresponding to the year 2024, describes the current state of AI as characterized by huge models and a wide range of applications. It lists specific examples including Chat-GPT, GPT-4, Gemini, Llama, open-source LLMs, Whisper, Robotics Transformer, Stable Diffusion, and Sora.

children.title: Future (?!)
children.summary: The section titled 'Future (?!)' is the final entry on an 'Attention Timeline' slide. It follows the 'Present Day' (2024) and marks the end of the timeline with a downward-pointing arrow, indicating that future developments in attention mechanisms are unknown or speculative.

children.title: What are transformers?
children.summary: This page explains the concept of transformers as a neural network architecture designed for 'composites' (things made of distinct parts). It defines composites and provides examples across three modalities: text (broken into words), images (broken into patches), and sound (broken into frames). The text on the right clarifies that these constituent elements are generically called 'tokens' and the process of breaking them down is known as 'tokenization'.

children.title: What can we do with transformers?
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/What can we do with transformers?
children.summary: The section titled 'What can we do with transformers?' outlines the diverse applications of transformer models across four main domains: Natural Language Processing (including text classification, summarization, and translation), Computer Vision (image classification and object detection), Audio (speech recognition), and Multimodal tasks (such as optical character recognition and visual question answering).

children.title: What can we do with transformers? Classify composites
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/What can we do with transformers? Classify composites
children.summary: This page illustrates the application of transformers for image classification, specifically focusing on classifying composite images. It presents a workflow where an input image of a cat is processed by an 'Image Classification Model' to produce output probabilities for different cat breeds. The example shows the model predicting a 0.514 probability for 'Egyptian cat', 0.193 for 'Tabby cat', and 0.068 for 'Tiger cat'.

children.title: Classify composites
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/What can we do with transformers? Classify composites/Classify composites
children.summary: The page illustrates a text classification task using transformers to classify composites. It presents a workflow where an input sentence, 'I love Hugging Face!', is processed by a Text Classification Model. The model outputs sentiment probabilities for three classes: POSITIVE (0.900), NEUTRAL (0.100), and NEGATIVE (0.000).

children.title: Complete composites
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/What can we do with transformers? Classify composites/Complete composites
children.summary: The page explains the concept of 'Complete composites' using transformers, specifically focusing on text generation via Causal Language Modeling. It illustrates an autoregressive process where a model takes an input (e.g., 'Once upon a time,') and generates output token by token. A diagram shows the progression from input to a full paragraph, while a step-by-step breakdown demonstrates how the model predicts subsequent words like 'My', 'name', 'is', and 'Sylvain'.

children.title: What can we do with transformers? Complete composites
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/What can we do with transformers? Complete composites
children.summary: The section titled 'What can we do with transformers?' outlines two main categories of tasks: 'Complete composites' and 'Transform composites'. The first category involves filling in missing tokens, exemplified by Masked Language Modeling (Fill-Mask) where a model predicts the most likely word for a masked token (e.g., predicting 'wolf' for 'The <mask> barked at me') and Image Inpainting, which reconstructs missing parts of an image. The second category involves transforming one composite into another, with Translation provided as an example, showing a sentence being translated from English to German.

children.title: What can we do with transformers? Transform composites
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/What can we do with transformers? Transform composites
children.summary: This section, titled 'Transform composites', explains the task of using transformers to convert a composite input into a different type of output. It provides three distinct examples: 1) Summarization, where a detailed text about the Eiffel Tower is condensed; 2) Image to Text, where an image of animals in a field is described with text; and 3) Text to Image, where a textual description of a city above clouds is used to generate an image.

children.title: How to classify composites with transformers?
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/How to classify composites with transformers?
children.summary: The page outlines a two-step process for classifying composites using transformers: first, obtaining a 'good' semantic representation of the composite, and second, using that representation to perform the classification. The slide concludes with a rhetorical question questioning the definition or nature of these representations.

children.title: Representations matter
children.summary: The page displays Figure 2, which illustrates the concept that data representations are crucial for machine learning models. It features two scatter plots: 'Cartesian Space (2d)' shows two classes of data points arranged in concentric circles, making them non-linearly separable. The adjacent plot, 'Feature Space', demonstrates how a simple transformation (squaring the raw features) linearizes the data, allowing for easy separation by a model like Logistic Regression.

children.title: Representation learning
children.summary: The page illustrates the concept of representation learning using a diagram that contrasts a 'Default Representation' with a 'Good Semantic Representation'. It shows how a Deep Neural Network processes input data (represented by cat and dog icons) to separate them into distinct clusters in a semantic space. The text at the bottom poses a question about building good representations for composites and suggests using an encoder based on transformer layers.

children.title: How can we build a “good” semantic representation for composites? Encoders
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/How can we build a “good” semantic representation for composites? Encoders
children.summary: The page outlines a two-step process for building a 'good' semantic representation for composites using encoders. The first step involves obtaining an initial, non-semantic representation of the composite. The second step is to feed this representation through several transformer layers.

children.title: How can be build a representation for composites?
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/How can be build a representation for composites?
children.summary: This slide explains how to build representations for composites by breaking them down into smaller units called tokens. It illustrates that text is composed of words, images are divided into patches, and sound signals are segmented into frames. The page concludes by defining the process of converting these tokens into vectors of real numbers as 'embedding'.

children.title: Embeddings
children.summary: The page defines 'Embeddings' as a method for representing tokens as points in a continuous vector space, where the spatial locations are semantically meaningful to machine learning (ML) algorithms. A diagram illustrates this concept by showing two clusters of points: one labeled 'high alignment' containing closely grouped items, and another point far away labeled 'low alignment', demonstrating how semantic similarity is represented by proximity in the vector space.

children.title: Word embeddings
children.summary: The page illustrates the concept of word embeddings using three-dimensional scatter plots to demonstrate semantic relationships. The first plot shows gender analogies (king-queen, man-woman), the second displays verb tense transformations (walking-walked, swimming-swam), and the third visualizes country-capital pairs across multiple nations.

children.title: How can we build a representation for composites?
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/How can we build a representation for composites?
children.summary: The section outlines a two-step process for building representations for composites. First, the composite text is tokenized into individual tokens (e.g., words or sub-words) and converted into initial vector embeddings. Second, these initial embeddings are fed through multiple layers of a Transformer Encoder to generate 'context-aware' semantic representations.

children.title: What are “context-aware” embeddings
children.summary: This page explains the concept of 'context-aware' embeddings, stating that a token's meaning depends on other tokens within a composite. It illustrates this with two examples: in the first sentence, 'it' refers to the 'road', while in the second, 'it' refers to the 'robot'.

children.title: How do transformer layers deal with context?
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/How do transformer layers deal with context?
children.summary: This section explains how transformer layers process context through the mechanism of attention. It outlines a three-step conceptual model: tokens exchange messages, each token calculates an 'attention' weight to determine how much to consider other tokens' messages, and finally, each token updates its embedding based on these weighted messages. The second page provides a visual example using the sentence 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired/wide', demonstrating how the word 'it' attends to different antecedents ('animal' vs 'street') depending on the context.

children.title: Text classification with transformers
children.summary: The page displays a diagram titled 'Text classification with transformers', illustrating the workflow of a transformer model. It details the process from tokenization (input sequence: 'this movie is great') through embedding, transformation via multiple transformer blocks, and finally to an output prediction ('pos' or 'neg') compared against a target.

children.title: Text classification with transformers using BERT
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Text classification with transformers using BERT
children.summary: The section titled 'Text classification with transformers using BERT' presents a diagram illustrating the architecture of a BERT model for text classification. The diagram shows input embeddings (including a special <class> token) combined with positional encodings, which are then processed through multiple stacked transformer layers. The output from these layers is passed to Label Smoothing Machines (LSM) to produce predictions. The page also cites the original BERT paper by Devlin et al. and the Deep Learning textbook by Bishop.

children.title: BERT training MLM
children.summary: The page explains the Masked Language Model (MLM) technique used in pre-training BERT. It features a diagram illustrating how the model takes an input sequence with a masked token ([MASK]) and predicts the original word based on surrounding context to output the most probable candidates. The text clarifies that typically around 15% of tokens are masked, and the objective is to predict these words using bidirectional context.

children.title: BERT training NSP
children.summary: The section titled 'BERT training NSP' illustrates the Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) task used to train BERT. It depicts a diagram where two sentences are fed into the BERT model, producing embeddings that are processed to generate a class label. The text explains that this process teaches BERT to understand longer-term dependencies across sentences.

children.title: Image classification with ViT
children.summary: The section titled 'Image classification with ViT' illustrates the architecture of a Vision Transformer (ViT) for image classification. It depicts the process where an input image is divided into patches, which are then linearly projected and combined with position embeddings. These embeddings, along with an extra learnable class embedding, are fed into a Transformer Encoder to produce final embeddings. The content cites the paper 'An Image Is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale' by Dosovitskiy et al.

children.title: How to generate composites? Decoders
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/How to generate composites? Decoders
children.summary: The section titled 'How to generate composites? Decoders' illustrates the operational differences between encoder-based models like BERT and decoder-based models like GPT. The first diagram contrasts BERT's masked language modeling approach, which fills in missing words from a sentence with randomly masked tokens, against GPT's autoregressive generation, which predicts the next word sequentially based on incomplete text. The second diagram details the internal architecture of a decoder model, showing a stack of L masked transformer layers that process input embeddings (including positional encoding) through multiple stages to produce output sequences via LogSoftmax (LSM) layers.

children.title: What is masked attention?
children.summary: The section titled 'What is masked attention?' explains the concept through two visual examples. The first example uses a sentence diagram to show how a token ('it') attends only to preceding words, preventing it from attending to future tokens (indicated by red crosses). The second example illustrates this using an attention matrix for the sentence 'Life is short eat desert first', demonstrating that in the row corresponding to 'Life', all attention weights for subsequent tokens are masked out (set to zero or ignored), ensuring the model only looks back at previous context.

children.title: How are decoders trained?
children.summary: This slide addresses the question of how decoders are trained, stating that the model is simply trained to predict the next word. On the right side, there is a citation for the book 'Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)' by Sebastian Raschka, published by Manning in 2024.

children.title: How are decoders efficiently trained?
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/How are decoders efficiently trained?
children.summary: This section explains the efficient training method for decoder models, specifically Large Language Models (LLMs). It illustrates that LLMs are trained to predict one word at a time in an autoregressive manner. The diagram shows how the model receives a sequence of words as input and predicts the next word in the sequence, with the constraint that it cannot access future words past the target.

children.title: Transforming composites. Encoders and decoders together
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Transforming composites. Encoders and decoders together
children.summary: The section titled 'Transforming composites. Encoders and decoders together' illustrates the architecture of a sequence-to-sequence model, likely for machine translation. It details an 8-step process where input text is preprocessed and fed into an Encoder to generate embeddings (steps 1-4). These embeddings are then passed to a Decoder, which generates translated output one word at a time based on partial outputs (steps 5-8). The diagram uses the example of translating 'This is an example' to 'Das ist ein Beispiel'. Additionally, the page cites Sebastian Raschka's book 'Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)' published by Manning in 2024.

children.title: Decoders vs. conditional decoders
children.summary: The page compares standard decoders with conditional decoders in the context of language models. It illustrates that a standard decoder approximates the probability of the next token based only on previous tokens, while a conditional decoder incorporates an additional condition 'c' (such as sentence meaning) to generate the output. The slide also references Sebastian Raschka's book "Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)" published by Manning in 2024.

children.title: Transforming composites.
children.summary: The section titled 'Transforming composites' illustrates a neural network architecture designed for sequence-to-sequence tasks, specifically using an encoder-decoder structure. The diagram details an 'encoder' that processes input X through embedding and self-attention transformer layers to produce representation Z. This is fed into a 'conditional decoder' which utilizes cross-attention transformer layers and a final LSM (likely Layer Softmax) to generate output Y_N based on previous outputs.

children.title: Opening the box. Understanding transformer layers.
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Opening the box. Understanding transformer layers.
children.summary: The page presents a conceptual breakdown of transformer architectures, mapping specific layer types to their functional roles. It identifies standard 'Transformer layers' as the basis for Encoders, 'Masked transformer layers' for Decoders, and 'Cross-attention transformer layers' for Conditional decoders.

children.title: Transformer layer
children.summary: The section titled 'Transformer layer' defines the architecture and operation of a single Transformer layer. It presents Algorithm 12.3, which details the input (a set of tokens X), parameters (multi-head self-attention and feed-forward network), and output (transformed tokens X̃). The algorithm describes two main steps: first, applying multi-head self-attention followed by an add-and-norm residual connection to produce Z; second, passing Z through a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with another add-and-norm step to produce the final output X̃. A diagram on the right visually represents this flow, showing the sequence from input X through multi-head self-attention, add & norm, MLP, and a final add & norm to yield X̃.

children.title: Attention coefficients
children.summary: This page explains the concept of attention coefficients in a mathematical context. It defines the coefficient a_nm as the amount token n attends to token m, subject to constraints that coefficients must be non-negative and sum to 1 (convex combination). The page also presents the matrix form Y = AX and provides a link to a Geogebra interactive tool.

children.title: How to compute attention weights
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/How to compute attention weights
children.summary: The page explains the process of computing attention weights in a model. It defines three components for each token: a query (q_i) representing what tokens it wants to receive, a key (k_i) representing what tokens it can send to, and a value (v_i) representing the message it distributes. The text concludes by stating that the attention weight between two tokens is calculated as the dot product of their respective query and key vectors.

children.title: Attention via linear transformations
children.summary: The page explains the concept of 'Attention via linear transformations' within a Transformer layer. It details how queries (Q), keys (K), and values (V) are computed from an input matrix X using independent linear transformation matrices W(q), W(k), and W(v). The content includes a flowchart illustrating the process, mathematical formulas for calculating Q, K, V, the attention matrix A, and the final output Y.

children.title: Softmax
children.summary: The page illustrates the Softmax function, showing a transformation of an input vector into a probability distribution. The input vector contains values [0.25, 1.23, -0.8], which are processed through a 'Softmax' block to produce the output vector [0.249, 0.664, 0.087].

children.title: Self-Attention
children.summary: This page illustrates the Self-Attention mechanism used in Transformer models. It breaks down the process into four main steps: Input Embedding, Queries, Keys, and Values. The diagram shows how input tokens (e.g., 'Thinking', 'Machines') are transformed into vectors (X1, X2) and then multiplied by weight matrices (W^Q, W^K, W^V) to produce Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) matrices.

children.title: Scaled self-attention in one slide. One attention head
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Scaled self-attention in one slide. One attention head
children.summary: The page presents a visual and algorithmic explanation of scaled self-attention for a single attention head. On the left, a flowchart illustrates the data processing steps: input X is multiplied by weight matrices to generate queries (Q), keys (K), and values (V). These are then processed through matrix multiplication, scaling, and softmax operations to produce the final output Y. On the right, Algorithm 12.1 formally defines the 'Scaled dot-product self-attention' process, specifying the mathematical inputs (tokens and weight matrices) and the step-by-step computation of Q, K, V, and the final attention mechanism.

children.title: Multi head attention
children.summary: This section explains the concept of multi-head attention, a core component of transformer models. It illustrates how multiple 'attention heads' can learn to focus on different aspects of the input data (e.g., color, taste, movement) in parallel. The process involves splitting the input into several heads, calculating self-attention for each head independently using query (Q), key (K), and value (V) matrices, concatenating the resulting outputs, and then applying a final linear transformation to produce the layer's output.

children.title: Masked transformer layer. A regular transformer layer but with masked attention.
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Masked transformer layer. A regular transformer layer but with masked attention.
children.summary: The page illustrates the architecture of a masked transformer layer, which is a standard transformer layer modified to include masked attention. It features a diagram showing the internal components: Masked Multi Self Attention, Layer Norm, and Feed Forward blocks. Additionally, it displays two matrices comparing attention weights before and after masking; the second matrix demonstrates how future tokens are hidden (masked out) for each position to ensure autoregressive generation.

children.title: Cross-attention
children.summary: The page displays a diagram titled 'Cross-attention' illustrating the architecture of an encoder-decoder model, likely for sequence-to-sequence tasks. It shows two main components: an Encoder on the left and a Decoder on the right, both repeated N times (indicated by 'Nx'). The Encoder processes input using multi-head attention and feed-forward layers with residual connections. The Decoder uses masked multi-head attention to attend to previous outputs, followed by cross-attention that takes keys and values from the Encoder, then another feed-forward layer.

children.title: Cross-Attention (e.g. Machine Translation)
children.summary: The page displays a diagram illustrating the concept of Cross-Attention, specifically in the context of Machine Translation. It depicts a sequence-to-sequence model where an input French sentence ('je suis etudiant') is processed alongside a generated English output sequence ('I am a student'). The diagram shows how attention mechanisms connect the encoder (processing the source language) to the decoder (generating the target language), highlighting the alignment between words like 'etudiant' and 'student'.

children.title: Cross-attention transformer layer
children.summary: The page illustrates the architecture of a 'Cross-attention transformer layer'. It details the flow of data from two distinct inputs (x1 and x2) through weight matrices to generate Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) vectors. These are used to compute an attention matrix via Softmax, which is then combined with the values to produce output Z. The diagram also depicts the surrounding residual connections and normalization steps typical in transformer models.

children.title: Transformer & Multi-Head Attention
children.summary: The page displays a diagram titled 'Transformer & Multi-Head Attention', which illustrates the architecture of the Transformer model. The figure depicts the flow from input embeddings and positional encoding through multiple layers of masked multi-head attention, feed-forward networks, and normalization, culminating in output probabilities via a linear layer and softmax. It is labeled as Figure 1 from the paper 'Attention Is All You Need'.

children.title: Transformers vs. RNNs
children.summary: The page presents a comparison between RNNs and Transformers, highlighting the challenges associated with RNNs versus the advantages of Transformers. The content is organized into a two-column table: the left column lists issues such as long-range dependencies, gradient vanishing/exploding, sequential processing limitations, and computational complexity for RNNs; the right column contrasts these with Transformer capabilities like modeling long-range dependencies without gradient issues, parallelizable computation, fewer training steps, and lower per-layer complexity.

children.title: Large Language Models
children.summary: This page provides an overview of Large Language Models (LLMs), defining them as scaled-up Transformer architectures with millions or billions of parameters. It details their training on massive general textual data using a 'next token prediction' objective and highlights emergent abilities like chain-of-thought reasoning. The content also notes the high computational costs involved and describes how larger models function as 'plug-and-play' systems capable of few-shot or zero-shot learning through in-context prompting.

children.title: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models
children.summary: This slide introduces the concept of 'Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models' (LLMs). It explains that emergent abilities are capabilities present in larger models but not smaller ones, which cannot be predicted by extrapolating from smaller model performance. The text describes this phenomenon as a 'phase transition' where performance remains near-random until a critical threshold is reached, after which it improves heavily.

children.title: Few-Shot Prompting
children.summary: The page illustrates the concept of 'Few-Shot Prompting' using a language model. Figure 1 provides a concrete example where a model predicts sentiment based on provided input reviews. Figure 2 displays eight line charts demonstrating the emergence of task performance in various benchmarks (such as Mod. arithmetic, IPA transliterate, and Word unscramble) as the model scale (training FLOPs) increases. The caption explains that these graphs show how models achieve random performance until a certain scale is reached, after which performance significantly improves.

children.title: Potential Explanations of Emergence
children.summary: This slide, titled 'Potential Explanations of Emergence', discusses the lack of clear explanations for why certain abilities emerge in AI models. It suggests that evaluation metrics may not fully explain these phenomena and includes a disclaimer questioning if emergent abilities are merely a mirage. A quote from an arXiv paper is cited to support the idea that these abilities might result from metric choices rather than fundamental changes in model behavior.

children.title: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF)
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF)
children.summary: This page defines Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) as a technique that trains a reward model using human feedback to optimize an agent's policy. It explains the process of asking humans to rank instances of agent behavior and includes a diagram illustrating the interaction between the RL Algorithm, Environment, and Reward Predictor.

children.title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
children.summary: The page presents a comparison between Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). It features a diagram illustrating that while RLHF involves training a reward model and using reinforcement learning to optimize a policy, DPO directly optimizes the language model for human preferences using maximum likelihood estimation without an explicit reward function or RL. The text explains that DPO simplifies the fine-tuning process by avoiding the intermediate steps required in existing methods.

children.title: GPT-4
children.summary: This slide outlines the key features and capabilities of GPT-4, including its training methodology (supervised learning, RLHF, RLAIF) and multimodal nature which allows it to process both images and text. It highlights improvements over GPT-3.5 in reliability and nuance, specifies context window sizes of 8,192 and 32,768 tokens, notes strong performance on standardized tests, and mentions that technical details were not released.

children.title: Gemini
children.summary: The section titled 'Gemini' outlines the features and architecture of the Gemini model family. It highlights that the latest version is Gemini 1.5 Pro and notes that Gemini Ultra outperforms ChatGPT on most academic benchmarks. The text describes Gemini's ability to process multimodal data (text, audio, image, video) and its foundation on a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model, which improves efficiency. The second page elaborates on the MoE architecture, explaining it as a combination of specialized neural networks ('Experts') managed by a 'Gating network' that predicts the best response for a request.

children.title: Where we are (2024)
children.summary: The page is a presentation slide titled 'Where we are (2024)' that outlines recent advancements in artificial intelligence. It lists key developments such as the LLM boom featuring models like ChatGPT and GPT-4, progress in human alignment and ethics, and the rise of diffusion models for text-to-image generation. The right side features two figures: one summarizing ChatGPT's capabilities and limitations with an image source link to OpenAI, and another showing AI-generated images of avocado-shaped armchairs based on a text prompt.

children.title: The Future (What’s Next?)
children.summary: This slide, titled 'The Future (What's Next?)', outlines potential future applications and impacts of advanced AI. It lists capabilities such as generalist agents, long video understanding, and domain-specific foundation models like DoctorGPT. The slide also details real-world impacts including personalized education, healthcare diagnostics, multilingual communication, and interactive gaming.

children.title: The Future (What’s Missing?)
children.summary: This slide, titled 'The Future (What’s Missing?)', outlines a list of missing ingredients required to achieve Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) or Artificial Superintelligence (ASI). The bullet points cover technical and cognitive gaps such as reducing computation complexity, enhancing human controllability, aligning with language models of the human brain, adaptive learning, multi-sensory multimodal embodiment, infinite memory capabilities like Neural Turing Machines, self-improvement, autonomy, emotional intelligence, and ethical reasoning.

children.title: Questions?
children.summary: This page is a presentation slide titled 'Questions?' featuring an illustration of three red, devil-like figures. The figures are depicted in the style of the 'see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil' monkeys, with one covering its eyes, another its ears, and the third its mouth. A banner across the bottom reads 'ASK NO QUESTIONS, HEAR NO LIES'. The slide is numbered 85.

children.title: Hugging face
children.summary: The page displays a title 'Hugging face' and provides a hyperlink to a Medium article. The link points to an introduction to Hugging Face written by Anthony DeMey, serving as a starter's guide for using online models.

children.title: Transformers and LLMs: An Introduction
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Transformers and LLMs: An Introduction
children.summary: Transformers and LLMs: An Introduction 87

children.title: Challenges of NLP:
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Challenges and Weaknesses/Challenges of NLP:
children.summary: The section outlines the inherent challenges of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Key points include the discrete nature of text, the difficulty of data augmentation compared to other modalities, and the precision required where a single wrong word can alter meaning. It also highlights the potential for handling long context lengths and memories, such as in conversations.

children.title: Weaknesses of earlier models/apporoaches:
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Challenges and Weaknesses/Weaknesses of earlier models∕apporoaches:
children.summary: This section outlines the weaknesses of earlier models and approaches in NLP, specifically highlighting their short context length, reliance on 'linear' reasoning without attention mechanisms to focus on other parts, and the inability of methods like word2vec to adapt based on context.

children.title: NLP Throughout the Years
children.summary: NLP Throughout the Years

children.title: Rule Based NLP Systems
children.summary: The page displays a slide titled 'Rule Based NLP Systems' featuring an ASCII art representation of the word 'ELIZA'. The content describes Eliza as a mock Rogerian psychotherapist, originally created by Joseph Weizenbaum in 1966 at MIT. A sample dialogue between the user and the ELIZA program is shown, illustrating its conversational capabilities.

children.title: Linguistic Foundations
children.summary: The section titled 'Linguistic Foundations SIMPLE RULE BASED RULE' introduces rule-based approaches to semantic parsing and analyzing linguistic structure. It features a flowchart illustrating a simple rule-based system that processes input phrases like 'take call', 'accept call', or 'join call' to execute commands, alongside syntactic tree diagrams (constituency and dependency) for the sentence 'I prefer the morning flight through Denver'.

children.title: Seq2seq Models
children.summary: This page presents an overview of Seq2seq Models, specifically focusing on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory Networks (LSTMs). It highlights concepts such as token dependency, information flow, and the role of gates in controlling memory. The visual content includes a detailed diagram of an LSTM cell structure in the top right and a schematic illustrating the unrolling of an RNN over time steps at the bottom.

children.title: Attention and Transformers
children.summary: This page explains the concept of attention mechanisms in Transformers, detailing how they allow models to focus on specific aspects of input text using parameters called 'weights'. It describes that these weights are computed from the input and hidden states via a dot product of query, key, and value matrices followed by a softmax function. The slide includes the mathematical formula for scaled dot-product attention and a diagram illustrating an attention visualization where tokens like 'it_' attend to previous words.

children.title: Analogy for Q, K, V
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Analogy for Q, K, V
children.summary: This section uses a library system analogy to explain the roles of Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) in an attention mechanism. A user's query for information is matched against book summaries (keys) to find relevant books, from which detailed information (values) is retrieved. The text clarifies that this process involves a 'soft match' across multiple values, weighted by relevance, as formalized by the attention formula shown at the bottom.

children.title: Beyond Scaling
children.summary: This page, titled 'Beyond Scaling', discusses the potential for Large Models (LMs) to acquire new emergent abilities through continued scaling. It notes that while scaling is a key factor, it is not the only one; other elements like better architectures, data quality, and training procedures can also enable these abilities in smaller models. The slide concludes by suggesting future research directions such as improving few-shot prompting, theoretical work, and computational linguistics.

children.title: Questions for the Group
children.summary: The page displays a slide titled 'Questions for the Group' containing three discussion points regarding artificial intelligence research. The questions address the future of emergent abilities with increased scale, the trend of larger models and data versus creativity, and the comparison between retrieval-augmented systems versus learning everything within model parameters.

children.title: RLHF, ChatGPT, GPT-4, Gemini
children.summary: The section defines Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) as a technique that trains a reward model from human feedback to optimize an agent's policy. It includes a diagram illustrating the RLHF process involving a reward predictor, RL algorithm, and environment. The content then introduces Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), contrasting it with RLHF by explaining that DPO optimizes for human preferences directly without requiring an explicit reward function or reinforcement learning loop.

children.title: ChatGPT
children.summary: This section describes ChatGPT as a model finetuned on the GPT-3.5 series, which was trained using instruction tuning and RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback). It notes that ChatGPT has become extremely popular. A diagram illustrates the lineage of models leading to ChatGPT, starting from GPT-3 Initial (Davinci) through various Codex and InstructGPT versions, culminating in the GPT-3.5 Series.

children.title: Major Applications of Transformers
children.summary: Major Applications of Transformers

children.title: Text and Language
children.summary: The page is titled 'Text and Language' and features a central illustration of a chat interface with ChatGPT. The dialogue shows the AI identifying itself as a large language model trained by OpenAI designed to process human-like language, and clarifying that it is not human. Decorative elements include floating speech bubbles and icons connected by lines.

children.title: Audio: Speech + Music
children.summary: The page is a presentation slide titled "Audio: Speech + Music". It features a central graphic with a purple and blue wave pattern, overlaid with the text "OpenAI/Whisper" and the OpenAI logo.

children.title: Vision: Analyzing Images & Videos
children.summary: The page is a presentation slide titled 'Vision: Analyzing Images & Videos' that demonstrates object detection capabilities. It features an image of the Castel Sant'Angelo in Rome, overlaid with bounding boxes identifying specific elements. Red boxes labeled 'OBJECT' highlight architectural details like statues and lampposts, while yellow boxes labeled 'PERSON' identify individuals walking on the bridge.

children.title: Vision: Generating Images & Video
children.summary: The page is titled 'Vision: Generating Images & Video' and features a grid of 15 diverse AI-generated images, including portraits, landscapes, animals, and fantasy scenes. The bottom text categorizes the tools used for these visuals, listing image generators like Stable Diffusion, Dall-E, and Midjourney, as well as video models such as Sora and Pika.

children.title: Robotics, Simulations, Physical Tasks
children.summary: The page is titled 'Robotics, Simulations, Physical Tasks' and illustrates examples of AI agents performing complex tasks. The top section displays a grid of screenshots from the game Minecraft, showing tasks such as mining amethyst, gathering cactus, building houses, and fighting enemies. The bottom section features a photograph of a person operating a robotic arm setup (Mobile ALOHA) alongside a grid of images demonstrating learned policies for physical manipulation, including cooking shrimp, pushing chairs, and using a cabinet.

children.title: Playing Games
children.summary: This slide, titled 'Playing Games', illustrates the application of artificial intelligence in gaming. It features images related to AlphaGo (including a movie poster), DeepMind's work on StarCraft, and OpenAI Five playing Dota 2. The text highlights examples such as AlphaGo, AlphaStar, and AI for MOBA games like Dota 2 and League of Legends.

children.title: Biology + Healthcare
children.summary: The page illustrates the intersection of biology and healthcare, focusing on Google's Med-PaLM M model. A diagram details its capabilities across various medical modalities such as genomics, radiography, dermatology, and pathology, alongside tasks like question answering and report generation. The right side features promotional imagery for 'Med-PaLM 2' and a logo for Google DeepMind.

children.title: Recent Trends and Remaining Weaknesses of LLMs
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Recent Trends and Remaining Weaknesses of LLMs
children.summary: Recent Trends and Remaining Weaknesses of LLMs

children.title: Requiring Large Amounts of Data, Compute, and Cost
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Requiring Large Amounts of Data, Compute, and Cost
children.summary: This slide outlines the significant resource requirements for training current Large Language Models (LLMs), noting that they demand immense amounts of data, compute power, and financial cost. It specifies that training often spans weeks or months using thousands of GPUs. The page concludes by introducing the 'BabyLM challenge,' which questions whether LLMs can be trained on data volumes comparable to what a human child is exposed to during development.

children.title: BabyLM: Children vs. LLMs
children.summary: This section, titled 'BabyLM: Children vs. LLMs', outlines the differences between how children and Large Language Models (LLMs) learn language. It posits that LLMs rely on statistical learning requiring vast data, whereas children may use smarter, compositional methods. The content references ideas from Michael C. Frank's tweet to highlight a 4-5 order of magnitude difference in input required for emergence between humans and LLMs. A graph illustrates this gap by comparing human input bounds against models like PaLM and GPT-3 over age. Finally, it lists four factors contributing to these differences: innate knowledge/priors, multimodal grounding, active social learning, and evaluation differences.

children.title: Minified LLMs and On-Device LLMs
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Minified LLMs and On-Device LLMs
children.summary: This slide outlines the trend of using Large Language Models (LLMs) for everyday applications, emphasizing the need for them to run quickly on devices. It mentions current work on smaller open-source models like LLaMA and Mistral as alternatives to AutoGPT and ChatGPT plug-ins. The content highlights a future where users can fine-tune and run these models locally on their phones, noting that while open-source availability helps, the models remain large and expensive.

children.title: Memory Augmentation & Personalization
children.summary: The section discusses the limitations of Large Language Models (LLMs) regarding static knowledge and lack of personalization. It outlines potential approaches to memory augmentation, including memory banks, prefix-tuning, prompt-based methods, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). RAG is highlighted as a method that relies on external data stores to augment context, suitable for facts but not fundamental skills.

children.title: Pretraining Data Synthesis & Selection
children.summary: This slide discusses the current trends in pretraining data synthesis and selection, focusing on using synthetic data generated by models like GPT-4 to train smaller or peer models. It explains the concept of model distillation, where knowledge is transferred from a large 'Teacher' model to a more efficient 'Student' model to achieve similar performance with lower computational costs. The content cites Microsoft's Phi models as an example and references external resources, including an arXiv paper and Nathan Lambert's newsletter.

children.title: Microsoft Phi-2 Model
children.summary: This slide introduces the Microsoft Phi-2 Model, a 2.7 billion-parameter AI model designed to excel in reasoning and language understanding despite its smaller size compared to other models. It highlights that the model is trained on 'textbook-quality' data and synthetic datasets to teach common sense and general knowledge, including science and daily activities. The content also notes that the model serves as a resource for research into interpretability, safety improvements, and fine-tuning.

children.title: New Knowledge or “Memorizing”?
children.summary: This slide discusses the debate surrounding whether Large Language Models (LLMs) generate truly novel knowledge or simply memorize and regurgitate existing information. It outlines key concepts such as 'Innovation vs. Regurgitation,' 'Test-time Contamination' regarding training data overlap, and 'Cognitive Simulation.' The page concludes by highlighting ethical and practical implications, specifically citing a copyright lawsuit between the New York Times and OpenAI.

children.title: Continual Learning
children.summary: This page defines 'Continual Learning' as a form of infinite, permanent self-improvement similar to human learning. It discusses current research efforts involving finetuning small models using traces from better models or the same model after filtering. The text also mentions specific datasets and papers like UltraChat-200k, Zephyr, and the 'LLMs Can Self-Improve' paper as examples of work in this area.

children.title: Interpretability of LLMs
children.summary: This page outlines the concept of interpretability in Large Language Models (LLMs), describing them as complex 'black-box' systems due to their massive parameters and data. It emphasizes the need for further research into mechanistic interpretability to better understand model components, improve control, and ensure safety.

children.title: Model Editing & Mechanistic Interpretability
children.summary: This slide outlines research on mechanistic interpretability and model editing, specifically focusing on the Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method. It describes a causal intervention technique used to trace decisive neuron activations for factual predictions in language models. The page includes Figure 1, which visualizes causal traces by comparing clean states against corrupted inputs to identify how specific layers (MLP vs. Attention) impact output probability.

children.title: Model Modularity + Mixture of Experts (MoE)
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Model Modularity + Mixture of Experts (MoE)
children.summary: This section discusses Model Modularity and Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures. It highlights the prevalence of MoE in modern Large Language Models like GPT-4 and Gemini, where specialized 'experts' collaborate to solve problems. The text also explores a variation involving segmenting a single neural network into different functional compartments (e.g., for fact-based info or spatial reasoning) similar to the human brain, or adding specific layers on top of a foundation model to tune for new domains.

children.title: Self-Improvement / Self-Reflection
children.summary: This section discusses the concept of self-improvement and self-reflection in AI models, where models reflect on their own outputs to iteratively refine them. It lists examples of works such as ReAct, Reflexion, and Self-refine, and mentions training LMs with language feedback. The text hypothesizes that results improve up to a point before degrading, depending on model scale and task, and notes the belief that AGI is a 'constant state of self-reflection'. A diagram illustrates how reflection can be added to decision-making approaches like ReAct agents, and a chart shows performance improvements on the SQuAD benchmark using these methods.

children.title: Hallucination Problem
children.summary: This page outlines the 'Hallucination Problem' in AI models, describing how they generate confident but factually incorrect text due to their sampling procedures. It suggests several methods to mitigate this issue, including enhancing retrieval (e.g., via Google), internal fact verification, output regeneration, modifying token sampling, and predicting hallucinations before generation.

children.title: Reasoning: Sufficient? Intermediate Guidance Helps...
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Reasoning: Sufficient? Intermediate Guidance Helps...
children.summary: This slide introduces the concept of Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, describing it as a series of intermediate steps inspired by human thought processes. It highlights that CoT improves Large Language Model (LLM) performance on complex tasks and provides an interpretable window into how models arrive at answers. The content concludes by noting that CoT leverages the model's internal knowledge more effectively than simple prompting.

children.title: Standard Prompting
children.summary: The 'Standard Prompting' section illustrates a model's input and output for two math word problems. The first problem asks for the total number of tennis balls Roger has after buying more, where the model correctly answers 11. The second problem involves calculating the remaining apples in a cafeteria after usage and restocking; here, the model incorrectly calculates the answer as 27.

children.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
children.summary: The section titled 'Chain-of-Thought Reasoning' compares 'Standard Prompting' with 'Chain-of-Thought Prompting'. It demonstrates that while standard prompting often leads to incorrect answers for multi-step math problems (like the apple example resulting in 27), chain-of-thought prompting guides the model to show its intermediate reasoning steps. This explicit breakdown of logic allows the model to arrive at the correct answer (9) by following a clear sequence of calculations.

children.title: Improving Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
children.summary: This slide discusses the limitations of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in large language models (LMs), noting that while it improves performance, errors persist. It provides a breakdown of these errors, attributing 8% to calculator mistakes, 16% to symbol mapping issues, and 22% to missing steps, with the remainder caused by semantic understanding problems. The page concludes by suggesting future investigation into methods to address these specific error types.

children.title: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Smaller Models
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Smaller Models
children.summary: This slide discusses the application of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to smaller AI models. It notes that CoT is currently effective for large models (approx. 100B parameters) but identifies common errors in smaller models, such as 'one-step missing' and 'semantic understanding' issues. The page lists three potential reasons for these failures: difficulty with symbol mapping, weaker arithmetic abilities, and logical loopholes. Finally, it emphasizes the significant value of improving CoT for smaller models to the research community.

children.title: Generalizing Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
children.summary: The page presents a slide titled 'Generalizing Chain-of-Thought Reasoning' that outlines the limitations of standard CoT, such as its rigid definition and limited applicability to specific domains. It contrasts this with human reasoning, which is flexible and multi-faceted, and proposes a more open 'scratchpad' approach to generalize CoT.

children.title: Tree of Thoughts
children.summary: The page introduces the 'Tree of Thoughts' (ToT) method, defining it as a process that considers multiple reasoning paths and self-evaluating choices to make global decisions. It includes Figure 1, which schematically illustrates four problem-solving approaches for Large Language Models (LLMs): Input-Output Prompting, Chain of Thought Prompting, Self Consistency with CoT, and Tree of Thoughts. The figure depicts how ToT explores a tree-like structure of thoughts compared to linear or voting-based methods.

children.title: Socratic Questioning
children.summary: The page introduces the 'Socratic Questioning' framework, described as a divide-and-conquer algorithm that simulates self-questioning and recursive thinking using large-scale language models. Figure 1 illustrates an example of this process solving a visual question about balloons by breaking it down into sub-questions. Figure 2 provides a technical overview of the Socratic Questioning (SQ) framework architecture, detailing the thought backtracking mechanism and variable definitions.

children.title: From Language Models to AI Agents
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/From Language Models to AI Agents
children.summary: The image displays a presentation slide with a dark gradient background. The main content is the title text 'From Language Models to AI Agents' centered in large white font.

children.title: Introduction
children.summary: This page serves as an introduction to a presentation on AI agents. It lists six key topics: Actions and Emergent Agent Architectures, Building Human-like AI Agents, Computer Interactions using AI, Long-Term Memory and Personalization, Agent to Agent communication, and Future Directions for Autonomous AI Agents. A cartoon robot illustration is displayed on the right side.

children.title: Building AI Agents
children.summary: This slide, titled 'Building AI Agents', outlines a presentation agenda covering the reasons for building agents, methods, ingredients, and capabilities. It presents a key thesis that humans will communicate with AI via natural language to operate machines more intuitively. The page also features an image of a processor chip labeled 'OpenAI INSIDE GPT 4' and includes the text 'Software 3.0'.

children.title: AI Agents
children.summary: The section titled 'AI Agents' outlines the rationale, methodology, and components of AI agents. It explains that single calls to foundation models are insufficient and that building AI systems unlocks more potential. The text details how these systems work through model chaining and reflection, lists ingredients like memory and internet access, and poses questions about their capabilities. The accompanying diagram illustrates an agent architecture centered around an 'Agent' core connected to Memory (short-term and long-term), Tools (Calendar, Calculator, CodeInterpreter, Search), Action, and Planning (Reflection, Self-critics, Chain of thoughts, Subgoal decomposition).

children.title: The first flight to be fully booked by an AI
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/The first flight to be fully booked by an AI
children.summary: The page displays a presentation slide titled 'The first flight to be fully booked by an AI'. It features a screenshot of a web browser interface showing the 'MULTI-ON' tool, where a search query is entered to book a one-way flight from NYC to SFO for June 10 for the 'MULTION hackathon u'.

children.title: AI Agent Passing the Online CA Driving Test
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/AI Agent Passing the Online CA Driving Test
children.summary: The page features a presentation slide titled 'AI Agent Passing the Online CA Driving Test'. It displays an image of a laptop screen showing the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) online test interface. Accompanying text on the right announces that an AI agent has fully autonomously passed this official test, setting a record as the first AI to obtain a driving permit in California.

children.title: Why human-like AI Agents?
children.summary: The page is a presentation slide titled 'Why human-like AI Agents?' that outlines five key reasons for developing such agents. The points cover their ability to use existing interfaces, act as digital extensions of users, operate without API restrictions, utilize simple action primitives like clicking and typing, and possess self-learning capabilities.

children.title: 5 levels of Autonomy
children.summary: The page displays a chart titled '5 levels of Autonomy' for on-road vehicles, detailing the division of control between human drivers and automated systems across six levels (0 to 5). The table categorizes responsibilities into steering/acceleration, monitoring the environment, fallback during failure, and overall system control. It visually represents that Level 0 involves no automation, while Levels 1-2 offer partial assistance where the driver monitors the road, and Levels 3-5 represent conditional, high, and full automation respectively, where the system takes over more tasks.

children.title: Computer Interactions
children.summary: Computer Interactions

children.title: Agent Computer Interaction
children.summary: The slide titled 'Agent Computer Interaction' outlines two primary routes for agent interaction: API (programmatic) and Direct interaction (browser or desktop control). The API route is characterized by being easy to build context, safer & controllable, but having high variability. Conversely, the Direct interaction route allows for easy actions and free-form interactions but requires providing guarantees. Several logos are displayed as examples, including GORILLA, ChatGPT Plugins, MULTI-ON, and ADEPT.

children.title: Agent Action API: An universal API for computer interaction
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Agent Action API: An universal API for computer interaction
children.summary: The page displays a presentation slide titled 'Agent Action API: An universal API for computer interaction'. It features a screenshot of a Jupyter Notebook environment (langchain_example.ipynb) demonstrating Python code. The code illustrates how to use the 'multion' library to log in and make API calls, specifically showing an example of generating a tweet via the Twitter API. Additionally, it includes a section labeled 'LANGCHAIN EXAMPLE' that imports various components from the LangChain library, such as LLMs and agents.

children.title: Memory & Personalization
children.summary: Memory & Personalization

children.title: AI Models as Neural Compute Unit
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/AI Models as Neural Compute Unit
children.summary: The section titled 'AI Models as Neural Compute Unit' illustrates the concept of using AI models, specifically GPT-4, as a computational unit. The first image depicts a flow where input tokens are processed by an OpenAI chip to produce output tokens, drawing a parallel to traditional MIPS32 processor instructions. The second image details the architecture of 'Looped Transformers,' showing how a Transformer model processes an input embedding sequence composed of scratchpad, memory, and instructions, with feedback loops indicated.

children.title: Long-term Memory
children.summary: This slide outlines the concept of Long-term Memory, describing it as a system that functions similarly to disk storage due to its long-lived and persistent nature. It lists key mechanisms such as embeddings and retrieval models, and identifies open questions regarding hierarchy, temporal coherence, structure, and online adaptation. A simple diagram on the right depicts a cylinder labeled 'Memory'.

children.title: Personalization
children.summary: The page is a presentation slide titled 'Personalization' that defines the User-Agent Alignment Problem as enabling an agent to act in accordance with user preferences. It further categorizes these preferences into two types: Explicit (e.g., allergies, favorite dishes) and Implicit (e.g., brand choices or item rankings).

children.title: Challenges
children.summary: This page outlines key challenges in the context of user preference modeling. It details methods for collecting data, such as active asking versus passive learning, and discusses approaches to learning from preferences like supervised fine-tuning versus human feedback. The slide also lists on-fly adaptation and privacy as significant challenges.

children.title: Agent-to-Agent Communication
children.summary: Agent-to-Agent Communication

children.title: Multi Agent Autonomous AI systems
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Multi Agent Autonomous AI systems
children.summary: The page is a presentation slide titled 'Multi Agent Autonomous AI systems'. It features five identical cartoon-style robot icons arranged in two rows (two on top, three on the bottom) to visually represent multiple autonomous agents.

children.title: Why Multi-agent Systems
children.summary: The section titled 'Why Multi-agent Systems' outlines the primary benefits and challenges of using multi-agent architectures. Key advantages include parallelization, which improves efficiency by dividing tasks among agents, and task specialization, where specific agents handle distinct services like spreadsheets or web browsing. The section also identifies a major challenge: agent-to-agent communication, specifically the need for robust protocols to exchange information and request assistance between AI agents.

children.title: Future Directions
children.summary: Future Directions

children.title: Key Issues with Autonomous Agents
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Key Issues with Autonomous Agents
children.summary: The page displays a presentation slide titled 'Key Issues with Autonomous Agents'. It lists four main challenges: Reliability, Looping & Plan Divergence, Testing & Benchmarking, and Real world-deployment & Observability. The fourth point is further detailed with two sub-questions regarding trust in autonomous AI systems and the implementation of human overrides.

children.title: Plan Divergence
children.summary: The page displays a diagram titled 'Plan Divergence' illustrating the difference between an 'Ideal Path' (a straight white line) and an 'Actual path' (a fluctuating red line). The visual metaphor suggests that real-world execution often deviates significantly from the planned trajectory. A caption at the bottom states that AI Agents like AutoGPT do not know how to correct mistakes.

children.title: Karpathy - LLM OS
children.summary: The page displays a system architecture diagram titled 'Karpathy - LLM OS', illustrating how an operating system might be structured around a Large Language Model (LLM). The central component is the LLM, which acts as the CPU and contains RAM for the context window. It connects to various peripheral devices like video and audio, classical software tools such as Python interpreters and terminals, storage via a file system, and network resources including a browser and other LLMs.

children.title: Building Generalized AI Systems
children.summary: The page displays a system architecture diagram titled 'Building Generalized AI Systems' for a component labeled 'Neural Computer'. The diagram illustrates a workflow where a User interacts via a Chat Interface, which feeds into a Task Engine. This engine processes inputs based on Rules and Reflection to generate a Task, which is then routed by a Router to external resources like the Web, Apps/Tools, or a Local Index before returning a Result.

children.title: Future needs for AI agents
children.path: Transformers Tutorial.pdf/Root/Future needs for AI agents
children.summary: The section titled 'Future needs for AI agents' outlines three key areas requiring development: error correction mechanisms and improved agent frameworks, security and user permission models, and sandboxing along with deployment strategies for risky settings.
